title: JavaScript OOP versus C# and TypeScript
hook: TypeScript classes look like C# in a slide deck, but the JavaScript runtime only has objects, prototype links, and functions. Interviews fail when you describe JavaScript OOP as nominal classes with virtual tables.

blocks.text: This topic compares **OOP** from the JavaScript runtime perspective versus C# and TypeScript. C# types are **nominal** — the Common Language Runtime (CLR) loads type names, access modifiers, interfaces, and virtual slots from Intermediate Language (IL) metadata. JavaScript has **objects and prototype chains**. TypeScript adds **structural** compile-time checks that **erase** in the emitted JavaScript.

entries.plainDefinition: Types match only with a declared relationship. C# uses nominal typing.
entries.example: CacheEntry and AuthHint are not interchangeable.

entries.plainDefinition: Compatible shapes assign freely. TypeScript at compile time.
entries.example: `const entry: CacheEntry = hint` allowed in TS.

entries.plainDefinition: Types removed during compilation. TS erases; C# preserves in IL.
Method lookup via prototype chain — mutable at runtime.

blocks.text: Server-side C# enforces `private` through CLR metadata. Client bundles are plain objects: TypeScript `private` is gone; only `#fields` give runtime hiding. C# records have value equality; browser JSON is plain objects with `===` reference semantics.

blocks.title: The one-sentence summary
blocks.body: The TypeScript compiler strips types. The CLR loads them. JavaScript runs whatever is left — objects, prototypes, and functions.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: JavaScript
items.body: Objects with [[Prototype]] links; methods found by lookup.

items.title: TypeScript
items.body: tsc removes interfaces and access modifiers.

items.title: C#
items.body: Roslyn emits IL with metadata; JIT uses it for is/as and virtual dispatch.

items.title: Runtime checks
items.body: C#: `is LtiHandler`. JS: `instanceof` on classes only — not TS interfaces.

snippet.label: Structural typing — TS allows, C# rejects
snippet.explanation: Structural assign at compile time; runtime is one plain object.

snippet.label: Nominal typing — CLR rejects unrelated types
snippet.explanation: Same shape, different CLR types — must copy explicitly.

snippet.label: Prototype dispatch versus virtual table
snippet.explanation: Polymorphism via prototype chain, not fixed vtable.

snippet.label: No runtime TypeScript interface
snippet.explanation: instanceof works for classes; interface names do not exist at runtime.

blocks.title: Equating TS private with C# private
blocks.body: TS private erases in the bundle. C# private is CLR-enforced. JS #field is runtime-enforced per class.

blocks.title: instanceof on TypeScript interfaces
blocks.body: Interface names throw ReferenceError — they were erased during compilation.

blocks.text: From the JS side: everything is an object graph with optional class sugar and erased TS annotations. .NET stack traces show `IAttemptStore.SaveAsync`; Node traces show `saveAsync` on a prototype — never erased interface names. Map keys use SameValueZero, not GetHashCode. Cross-language APIs: enforce nominal boundaries on server; client bundle is structurally typed at best.

snippet.label: Duck typing — no compiler guarantee
snippet.explanation: Works at runtime but lacks C# contract enforcement from interfaces.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying all three languages have the same class model at runtime. Claiming TS private is runtime-enforced. Saying JS has C# virtual dispatch.

interviewTakeaways: JavaScript runtime: objects, prototype chain, functions — no CLR metadata.
TypeScript types erase; interfaces and private do not exist in the bundle unless #.
C# is nominal with virtual dispatch and value types; JS uses prototype lookup.

60s: JS runs objects and prototypes. TS adds erased structural types. CLR keeps metadata — private, interfaces, virtual slots. instanceof for JS classes not TS interfaces. Privacy: # runtime, TS erased, C# CLR.
Follow-up: assignment TS allows that C# rejects.
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'TS classes equal C# at runtime.' Strong: TS erases to constructor + prototype.
Treating prototype lookup as C# virtual dispatch.

jsTsCorrelations.note: The TypeScript compiler strips types. The CLR loads them. JavaScript runs the erased output.
C# keeps interfaces and access modifiers at runtime; JavaScript has duck typing and # fields only.
